title: Missing the band, and young fans at Ziegfeld's
summary: Booking keeps him close to young musicians; at Ziegfeld's Basie salutes him and young people swarm his table.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: (Side B of Tape 6 begins at this point.)

You know, it's said of Duke Ellington, and I'm sure this is evident in the case of Count Basie, they said if Duke-- when he started getting in his seventies, that if he didn't hear the sound of that band in his ears, he would die, I think that's why Basie stays out there. It's possible that Basie needs the money, Duke didn't. I think if Basie couldn't hear that band, play with that band and all that goes with it, I also suspect the glamour and the public attention has to do with it, how do you feel that you're no longer in it? Do you miss it, would you still like to be in the band business as a leader and a musician?

I think it would help a lot, and believe it or not, the booking--just the contact of being around the musicians, especially the young ones, it helps keep me alive. It's something that helps; I know when I was travelling, I kind of got big enough that
they would be saying to give an autograph, but that never did bother me. I said when they stop asking that's when I'll worry.

I really got a big kick here last (inaudible); Count was in town and Count made a short talk, he was in Ziegfeld's, and he was saying about his friend Ernie Fields is here and about the years that he's known, and so on, and then some of the oldtimers stood up and were clapping, but then the young ones just swarmed my table, I heard mama say something about you, I heard dad say about you. Those eighteen and twenty year olds had heard their people say something about me, and it's just something that gives you a lift.
She was probably very proud of that.
